scores.evidence: With Yjs, its built-in snapshots require turning off garbage collection, which makes documents bigger.
scores.rationale: Claims are accurate (Yjs snapshots/GC, relative positions, OT vs CRDT tradeoffs) and reach some subtle areas, though 'cheap with a CRDT' and 'free them from memory' are a bit glib.

scores.evidence: Get a thin end-to-end version working early, and add features only once the things they depend on exist.
scores.rationale: Covers core needs with sensible sequencing and explicit deferrals, but leaves targets and scale unspecified and is more a build order than a resolved design.

scores.evidence: Use a placeholder user ID for now... This needs the real user identities from step 5.
scores.rationale: Dependencies and ownership are consistent; minor loose ends, e.g. the Phase 1 single-user editor and the undo note 'fix it soon after step 3' placed in Phase 2.

scores.evidence: run randomized tests with several in-memory copies of the document, sending edits late, out of order and twice. Done when: thousands of random runs all end with identical copies.
scores.rationale: Riskiest merge correctness is tested early with checkable criteria and hash-drift detection in production, but load and perf criteria are not quantified.

scores.evidence: Targets: how many editors per document, maximum document size, acceptable delay, and whether you need offline editing and version history.
scores.rationale: Unknowns are listed as decisions to make, with conditional branches, but no concrete defaults or sensitivity analysis are given.

scores.evidence: Detect when copies drift apart by having clients compare hashes of the document.
scores.rationale: Covers adversarial input (schema, size, rate limits), reconnects, drift and fault tests, but detection and recovery are thin and revocation, corruption and poison updates are not addressed.

scores.evidence: Metrics such as how long edits take to reach other users, how often clients reconnect and how long documents take to load.
scores.rationale: Only metrics are mentioned; no deployment, rollback, migration, alerting or ownership plan.
Cost is barely addressed beyond a build-vs-hosted shortcut and storage growth from disabled GC.

scores.evidence: settle the hard-to-reverse decisions first... If you change it later, you have to migrate every stored document.
scores.rationale: Explicitly front-loads the hard-to-reverse choices (sync library, schema, history), though exit paths and schema versioning are not detailed.

scores.evidence: Shortcut: If you use Yjs + Tiptap + Hocuspocus (a ready-made Yjs server), or a hosted service like Liveblocks
scores.rationale: Starts simple, defers scale and product features, and recommends off-the-shelf parts; suggestion mode and the Redis option are reasonably deferred.

scores.evidence: Done when: two browsers can edit together live, and a dropped connection catches up with nothing lost.
scores.rationale: Ordered by dependencies with checkable done-criteria and parallelization, but some steps are vague and there is no contingency if early results disappoint.

checklist.evidence: Use Yjs by default. Pick OT only if you want one authoritative server and don't need offline editing.
Document schema: the block types, text formatting and embeds a document can contain.
sending edits late, out of order and twice. Done when: thousands of random runs all end with identical copies.
Store periodic snapshots plus a log of every edit, and shrink the log from time to time.
send everyone editing the same document to the same server, even if you start with only one server.
Keep a local copy in the browser (IndexedDB), queue edits while offline, merge them on reconnect
Enforce owner, editor, commenter and viewer roles on the server.
A restore should be applied as a new edit, never by rewriting the edit log.
over a separate channel that isn't saved.
Prove that edits made at the same time merge correctly before building anything on top.

traps.evidence: a CRDT (Yjs, Automerge) or OT/a central server that orders edits (ShareDB, prosemirror-collab)
Single-user editor on the real schema. Every edit goes through the document model
restarting the server loses no edit the server had confirmed.
This is cheap with a CRDT and hard with OT.

note: Strong risk-ordered build sequence with early convergence testing and durable logging; weak on operations, cost, protocol versioning and quantified assumptions.
